questions.q: What message does the summary say the early-achievement culture sends young people?
a: That they are failures if they have not succeeded by 30
That success requires a four-year college degree
That hard work matters far more than natural talent
That fame is the only goal worth pursuing
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes the unrealistic deadline that shames young people.

questions.q: What shift in goals does the summary blame for declining adolescent mental health?
a: A move from intrinsic goals toward extrinsic ones
A move from reading books to watching video
A decline in the average size of families
A rise in part-time jobs for teenagers
questions.why: Lesson 1 cites Jean Twenge's theory about valuing status, looks and scores.

questions.q: Which part of the brain develops last, according to the summary?
a: The prefrontal cortex
The cerebellum
The amygdala
The hippocampus
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the rational, planning part of the brain matures last.

questions.q: What happened to Karlgaard in his late twenties?
a: His mind seemed to wake up and he found direction
He inherited a business and became wealthy
He returned to school for a second degree
He moved abroad to start over completely
questions.why: Lesson 2 says his patience, ideas and writing ability suddenly developed.

questions.q: What does the summary advise if cultural pressure is steering your path?
a: Examine those influences and choose your own direction
Follow your family's plan until it clearly fails
Compare yourself with more successful peers
Wait until your thirties before deciding anything
questions.why: Lesson 3 uses Erik Wahl's reinvention to show the value of leaving others' expectations behind.
